cards.title: Query cost of reducing testing adaptivity
cards.formal: For testing an arbitrary Boolean property, how much can the universal query bound improve when a k-round-adaptive tester is replaced by an ℓ-round-adaptive tester, with 0≤ℓ<k? Writing q_j for the minimum query complexity at the same input length and proximity parameter, the source asks for a bound q_ℓ≤φ(q_k,ℓ,k) better than the general simulation q_ℓ≤2^{q_k}−1 when ℓ>0. A one-round reduction q_{k−1}≤q_k(1+2^{q_k/k}) is already proved. The source does not specify the amount or regime of improvement required of a general φ, so the quantitative target remains unfinished.
cards.why: Quantifies the general price of replacing sequential information gathering by fewer batches. A substantive universal bound would apply across Boolean property testing, beyond the behavior of one particular property.

importance.reason: A general resource tradeoff for adaptive Boolean property testing; a precise quantitative target is needed to distinguish a substantive advance from the existing simulations. Existing score retained.

sentences: The source asks how query complexity changes when a tester is allowed fewer batches of queries.
Its convention counts k rounds of adaptivity as k+1 actual batches.
A general exponential simulation and a better bound for removing one round are already known.
The requested new bound must cover arbitrary properties and allow the number of queries in each batch to depend on earlier answers.
The source leaves the amount and asymptotic regime of the desired improvement unspecified, which this card records explicitly.

cards.definitions:
Fix an integer n≥1, a nonempty property P⊆{0,1}ⁿ, and a proximity parameter ε∈(0,1]. An input f:[n]→{0,1} is available through a value oracle: a query i returns the single bit f(i). Its distance from P is min_{g∈P}|{i:f(i)≠g(i)}|/n. The tester must accept every f∈P with probability at least 2/3, and reject every input at distance strictly greater than ε with probability at least 2/3. On other inputs either verdict is allowed. Probabilities are over the tester’s internal random bits. This is ordinary two-sided testing with uniform Hamming distance, not tolerant testing, distribution testing or sample-only access.

Under the source’s convention, j rounds of adaptivity mean j+1 batches Q₀,…,Q_j. Each batch is chosen using internal randomness and the answers to all earlier batches. All locations in the current batch must be chosen before any of its answers are revealed. Batches may be empty. Both the identities of locations and the number of queries in a later batch may depend on earlier answers. Thus j=0 is a fully nonadaptive tester with one batch; j=1 permits two batches. The total number of value queries, summed over all batches and bounded on every input and random tape, is the cost. Local computation, descriptions of the property and query addresses are not charged as additional queries. Duplicate queries can be avoided or answered from stored values.

For this fixed n,P,ε, let q_j(n,P,ε) be the smallest worst-case number of queries used by a j-round-adaptive tester satisfying those guarantees. Algorithms are nonuniform in the source: for each n and known property they may be chosen separately. No polynomial running-time or uniform construction of testers from a succinct property description is required. Query budgets can always be capped at n by reading the entire input; extra empty rounds are harmless. The desired bound is universal over these Boolean properties and uses the same ε on both sides. Its function φ is to depend only on q_k,ℓ,k, with n,P,ε entering only through q_k.

Section 6.1 proves q_k≤q_ℓ≤2^{q_k}−1 for 0≤ℓ≤k and q_{k−1}≤q_k(1+2^{q_k/k}) for k>0. The first exponent is q_k; it is not the linear expression 2q_k−1. These are known universal upper bounds, not the unanswered result. Iterating the one-round inequality also supplies a bound for several removed rounds; the source’s wording does not select an explicit quantitative improvement over that consequence. Its remark stresses that general testers can adapt their batch sizes, so a theorem assuming a predetermined size for each batch would address only a special case.

The remaining task is to specify which joint regime of q_k,k,ℓ is being compared and what counts as a sufficient asymptotic improvement. The source does not demand matching lower bounds for an extremal tradeoff function, nor does it state a particular exponent-saving conjecture. This card therefore does not certify either of those stronger replacements.
cards.answer_criterion: A completed statement must specify the asymptotic upper bound φ and the regime and precision in which it improves the known simulation. A valid universal result must preserve the property, proximity parameter, success probability, adaptive batch-size freedom and worst-case query convention. The existing one-round theorem alone is not new progress; an optimal upper-and-lower tradeoff would be a stronger task than the source explicitly states.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
